In the elections of September 2008, women won 56 percent of the seats in Rwanda's Chamber of Deputies, making it the first national parliament in the world with a female majority.

After the genocide women were the majority of survivors, and many had to run farms and households alone. The constitution of 2003 reserved at least 30 percent of posts in decision-making bodies for women, and the ruling party put women high on its lists.

The share rose further in later elections. Laws were changed to let women inherit land. Critics note that Rwanda's parliament has little power against Paul Kagame, but the change in who holds office has been lasting.
sum: In the elections of September 2008, women won 56 percent of the seats in Rwanda's Chamber of Deputies, making it the first national parliament in the world with a female majority.
